description: Building an interactive, web-based Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer to introduce young explorers to spaceflight through STEM mini-games and simulations. Handling core frontend development and game logic, but welcome collaborators interested in 2D art, UI/UX, storytelling, or educational design to make the experience even better!
summary: Artemis-X is a Pokémon-style pixel-art mission trainer that teaches kids how astronauts survive off-world. Players command an outpost across five worlds (Moon, Mars, Venus, Europa and Titan), reachable by their own spaceship. Each Sol they split limited power between oxygen, greenhouse food and radiation shielding, then watch hazards like dust storms, solar flares and Jupiter's radiation test their choices. Roaming crew members, rovers and hostile aliens fill the huge maps, and battles are won by answering short science questions. With 15 missions per world, a minimap and almost no reading, it turns life-support trade-offs into play for the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Artemis-X is a browser game built for the "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge. The player runs a lunar or planetary outpost and must keep the crew alive by managing life support, shielding, power and food. Each day (Sol) the player allocates a limited power budget between oxygen generation, the greenhouse and radiation shielding. The game then resolves the day with random hazards such as dust storms, solar flares and radiation, so bad trade-offs have visible consequences.

The player explores five very large maps (Moon, Mars, Venus, Europa, Titan) on foot and travels between them in a spaceship with a flight mini-game. Every world has about 15 missions (reach a site, collect ice, repair, quiz, defend), roaming NPC crew and rovers, and hostile aliens. Alien fights are turn-based, Pokémon-style, and the player wins by scanning and answering a short science question. A tracking arrow and a minimap guide the player, so there is very little text to read.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Teaches real mission-planning ideas (resource trade-offs, radiation, power limits, closed-loop food) through play instead of text.

- Designed for young learners: icon-based UI, large D-pad and A/B buttons, short prompts, chiptune audio.

- Runs in any browser on phone or laptop, with no install and no account, so it is easy to use in classrooms.

- Each planet has different hazards, which shows why a Moon base and a Europa base need different engineering choices.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

HTML5 Canvas, CSS and JavaScript (single self-contained file), the Web Audio API for sound and the Press Start 2P font. Everything (maps, sprites, lighting, shadows, music) is generated in code. There are no external game assets.

CREATIVITY AND DESIGN

We replaced a text-heavy prototype with a retro RPG format kids already understand. Dynamic lighting, shadows, particles and a day/night-style colour grade make the worlds feel alive.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

Age-appropriate difficulty, minimal reading, accessibility with large controls and clear objectives, performance on low-end phones, and scientific plausibility of hazards and resources.
